title: The real refuge (188–196)
hookLine: frightened people run to mountains, groves and shrines; the safe refuge is the three jewels and the four truths

lines: THE FRIDGE, THE PHONE, THE PLAN.
IT WORKS FOR ABOUT AN HOUR.
cards: Where does your mind run when you're scared? For some it's the fridge. For some it's the phone, scrolling until the feeling goes numb.
For some it's work, or a person, or a plan with seventeen backups. Plenty of us have a hiding spot, and it works, for about an hour. Then the fear comes back and finds us there.
Chapter fourteen closes with a list of places frightened people run to, and then a different kind of shelter.

teach.b: Verse one eighty-eight, in Max Müller's words: "Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees."
And one eighty-nine: "But that is not a safe refuge, that is not the best refuge." The verse isn't mocking anyone's shrine; Buddhists themselves honor the tree the Buddha sat beneath.
Its point is about fear: a place can't carry you out of pain. Then verse one ninety: "He who takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church".
That's Müller's Victorian English for three Pali words: Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, the awakened teacher, the teaching, and the community that practices it. Buddhists call them the three jewels.
Müller's Church is the Sangha: the community of monks and nuns, and in a wider sense, for many Buddhists, everyone walking the path. And the refuge isn't only in who you trust but in what you see.
Verse one ninety-one names it: the four noble truths, in Müller's words, "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain".
Seeing those clearly, verse one ninety-two says, is the safe refuge, the best refuge. You met the refuges on day one hundred twenty-three, as a practice.

In Pali the line runs Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge, then the same for the Dhamma and the Sangha, three times through; others say it in Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese or English.
Not a cave to hide in. A place to stand.

how: Buddhists across the world take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, reciting the formula three times in Pali or their own language, at ceremonies, at the start of practice and often daily at a home shrine.

o: the Buddha, his teaching, and the community
the three marks: change, pain, not-self
three gems placed on a Buddhist altar

games.q: match Müller's words to the Pali.

s: Müller's 'the Church' in verse 190 means the Sangha
his Victorian English for the community that practices the teaching.
the verse mocks people who honor sacred trees
its point is that a place can't carry you out of pain; Buddhists honor the Bodhi tree too.
the safe refuge in verse 191 includes seeing the four noble truths
pain, its origin, its ending, and the eightfold way.

games.q: you're frightened. the people around you are heading for the mountains, the forest, the sacred grove. what does verse 190 point to?
o: the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, and the four truths.
stay home and lock the doors.
games.why: "that is the safe refuge, that is the best refuge." not a hiding place, but a place to stand.

practice: Name, without judging, one place you run to when you're afraid, then sit with the three refuges: the awakened one, the possibility that a human mind can wake up; the teaching, the way things really are, pain and its causes and its ending; the community, the people who have walked, and are walking, this path beside you.
If you're Buddhist, you can quietly say the refuge line, Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi; if not, simply rest in whichever of the three feels most like solid ground.

wordCard.voice: Three jewels. The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, the teacher, the teaching and the community, named together as the true shelter from fear.

orig.note: Pali: refuge, shelter, protection — as in Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge.

carryVoice: Your line: a place to stand. Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and the four truths seen clearly. Day one hundred ninety-five, and counting.
